```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
here::i_am("posts/cps-participation/index.qmd")
POST_DIR <- here::here("posts", "cps-participation")
source(file.path(POST_DIR, "R", "analysis.R"))
a <- readRDS(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "analysis.rds"))
change_text <- function(x) {
  if (abs(x) < 0.05) return("approximately unchanged")
  sprintf("%.1f percentage %s %s", abs(x), ifelse(round(abs(x), 1) == 1, "point", "points"), ifelse(x > 0, "higher", "lower"))
}
rate_for <- function(year, group) {
  z <- a$annual$rate[a$annual$YEAR == year & a$annual$age_group == group]
  stopifnot(length(z) == 1)
  sprintf("%.1f", 100 * z)
}
youth_rates <- a$annual[a$annual$age_group == "16-24", ]
youth_drop_2020 <- 100 * (youth_rates$rate[youth_rates$YEAR == 2020] -
                          youth_rates$rate[youth_rates$YEAR == 2019])
changes <- a$changes
change_for <- function(group) {
  x <- changes$change_pp[changes$age_group == group]
  stopifnot(length(x) == 1)
  sprintf("%.1f", abs(x))
}
month_count <- nrow(unique(a$monthly[c("YEAR", "MONTH")]))
record_count <- tail(a$audit$records, 1)
share_for <- function(year, group) {
  x <- a$annual_shares$share[a$annual_shares$YEAR == year &
                             a$annual_shares$age_group == group]
  stopifnot(length(x) == 1)
  sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x)
}
base <- a$overall[a$overall$YEAR == 2019, ]
last <- a$overall[a$overall$YEAR == 2024, ]
observed_change <- 100 * (last$observed - base$observed)
adjusted_change <- 100 * (last$standardized - base$standardized)
age_mix_gap <- 100 * (last$standardized - last$observed)
```

## What does a labor-market recovery mean?

Overall labor-force participation in 2024 was `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * last$observed)`%, `r change_text(observed_change)` than its 2019 rate of `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * base$observed)`%. Yet participation among adults aged 25 to 54 was `r change_for("25-54")` percentage points above its 2019 level. **Did participation fall within age groups, or did the population's age mix change?** The answer changes how we interpret the apparent shortfall in the labor-market recovery.

Unlike unemployment, which counts jobseekers as a share of the labor force, participation counts workers and jobseekers as a share of the population. I use monthly IPUMS CPS microdata for civilians aged 16 and older from 2019 through 2024, apply [WTFINL sampling weights](https://cps.ipums.org/cps-action/variables/WTFINL) to represent the population, and average the twelve monthly rates for each annual estimate.

## First, compare recovery paths

```{r}
#| label: fig-trends
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Annual means of monthly weighted participation rates, expressed as changes from 2019. Panels use identical percentage-point scales; zero marks each group’s baseline."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels showing changes in participation from 2019 for four age groups, with a shared scale and a zero baseline."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "trends.png"))
```

Figure 1 shows changes from 2019 across four stages of working life. By 2024, participation among adults aged 25 to 54 was `r change_for("25-54")` percentage points above its baseline. Adults aged 55 to 64 gained `r change_for("55-64")` points, while those aged 16 to 24 were approximately unchanged, gaining `r change_for("16-24")` points. Adults aged 65 and older were the only group still below baseline, down `r change_for("65+")` points.

All four groups declined between 2019 and 2020. Adults aged 16 to 24 had the deepest drop, `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(youth_drop_2020))` percentage points. Their participation rebounded above baseline in 2023 before falling back toward it in 2024. The contrasting outcomes for adults aged 55 to 64 and those aged 65 and older show why treating all older adults as one group would hide part of the recovery.

## Next, look at who makes up the population

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-shares
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Changes in each age group's share of the civilian population aged 16 and older, using annual averages of monthly weighted shares."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars showing changes in age-group population shares from 2019 to 2024. The share aged 65 and older increased, while all three younger groups' shares decreased."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "age_shares.png"))
```

Figure 2 introduces the other part of the story. Adults aged 65 and older grew from `r share_for(2019, "65+")`% to `r share_for(2024, "65+")`% of the population in this analysis. The shares of the three younger groups fell. This matters because participation in 2024 was `r rate_for(2024, "65+")`% among adults aged 65 and older, compared with `r rate_for(2024, "25-54")`% among those aged 25 to 54. A growing share of people in a group with lower participation can pull down the overall rate even when participation improves within most groups.

## Finally, hold the age mix fixed

To separate these two influences, I calculate each month's overall rate twice. Let $s_{g,y,m}$ be age group $g$'s population share and $p_{g,y,m}$ its participation rate in year $y$, month $m$.

$$
P_{y,m}=\sum_g s_{g,y,m}p_{g,y,m}
\qquad\text{(observed)}
$$

$$
P^{\mathrm{fixed}}_{y,m}=\sum_g s_{g,2019,m}p_{g,y,m}
\qquad\text{(2019 age mix)}
$$

The second calculation keeps the same participation rates but substitutes the corresponding month's 2019 population shares. For example, January 2024 uses January 2019 shares. I then average each set of twelve monthly rates. Only the shares differ, so the gap isolates the composition effect under this calculation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-age-mix
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Overall participation changes, observed and standardized to 2019 age-group shares. Both series equal zero in 2019 by construction."
#| fig-alt: "Two lines comparing observed changes in overall participation with changes after fixing the four age-group shares at their 2019 values."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "age_mix.png"))
```

Figure 3 expresses both series as changes from their common 2019 baseline. With the age mix held fixed, participation in 2024 was `r change_text(adjusted_change)` than in 2019. The observed shortfall becomes a modest increase.

In levels, observed participation in 2024 was `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * last$observed)`%, compared with `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * last$standardized)`% using the 2019 age mix. The gap was `r sprintf("%.2f", age_mix_gap)` percentage points. That difference describes the contribution of changing age shares under this standardization.

## Takeaway and limits

The CPS has a complex rotating design, and [pandemic-era collection disruptions](https://cps.ipums.org/cps/covid19.shtml) complicate interpretation. These comparisons do not establish causes or statistical significance. Annual averages hide monthly changes, and broad age groups hide differences within them. This analysis does not follow a fixed cohort.

- Participation recovered differently across age groups, with adults aged 65 and older still below their 2019 rate.
- The population also shifted toward that older group, which has much lower participation.
- With the 2019 age mix held fixed, 2024 participation was `r change_text(adjusted_change)` than in 2019, instead of `r change_text(observed_change)`. Under this standardization, the shift toward older age groups more than accounts for the overall shortfall.

---

**Data:** Flood et al. (2025), [IPUMS CPS: Version 13.0](https://doi.org/10.18128/D030.V13.0), University of Minnesota. Basic Monthly samples, January 2019 through December 2024; extract created September 27, 2026. The analysis uses `r format(record_count, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)` eligible person-month observations, not unique individuals.

**Code and replication:** [Blog repository](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog). The post folder contains the R analysis, aggregate results, figures, and replication instructions. Raw microdata are excluded from Git.
